steps.label: Gallium carries ten 3d electrons
lines: Gallium comes just after the first
transition series, so it has ten 3d
electrons between its nucleus and its
steps.why: Gallium follows the ten transition elements, so its added electrons went into the 3d subshell. Writing the two configurations side by side shows the one difference the whole answer rests on.
common_mistakes: Writing gallium as [Ar]4s²4p¹ and leaving out 3d¹⁰. Those ten d electrons are the reason for the answer.
Placing gallium in the same period as aluminium. Gallium is one period lower.
steps.memory_tip: Gallium sits after the ten transition elements, so it carries a 3d¹⁰ shell that aluminium never had.
steps.margin_note: Write both configurations; the explanation follows from the 3d¹⁰.

steps.label: Poor shielding, stronger pull
lines: The 3d electrons are diffuse and shield
So the outermost electrons of gallium
feel a greater effective nuclear charge
and are held closer to the nucleus.
The atomic radius of gallium is therefore
steps.why: Shielding decides how much of the nuclear charge actually reaches the valence electrons. Poor shielding by 3d¹⁰ leaves a larger effective nuclear charge, and a stronger pull gives a smaller radius, even though gallium is in a lower period.
common_mistakes: Writing that gallium is smaller because it has fewer shells. It has more shells; the shielding is what settles the answer.
Saying the d electrons shield well. Diffuse d orbitals shield less than s and p orbitals do.
steps.memory_tip: Poor shielding, stronger pull, smaller atom.
steps.margin_note: The words poor shielding and effective nuclear charge both belong in this step.

insider_note: The configuration on its own does not answer the question; the shielding argument is what turns 3d¹⁰ into a smaller radius.
